Construct leave-out reference maps for two crossed factors

Source: R/reference_maps.R
reference_maps.Rd

Stores source maps and grouped sums once. References are evaluated on demand, without storing four full maps for every subject/item pair.

Usage

reference_maps(
  dens_tab,
  subject = "subject",
  item = "item",
  refs = c("self_item", "self_other_items", "others_item", "others_other_items"),
  space = c("log", "density"),
  floor = NULL,
  min_n = 1,
  density_var = "density",
  normalize = c("sum", "none"),
  transform = c("none", "log")
)

Arguments

dens_tab

Table with one map per subject/item pair. NULL maps are missing.

subject, item

Names of the two crossed-factor columns.

refs

Requested reference names (see Details).

space

Average log values or density values.

floor

Explicit positive additive offset required when space = "log" (the default) or transform = "log". For unit-sum maps, a starting choice is 1 / (10 * ncells), where ncells is the number of grid cells. There is no automatic offset because this choice changes the reference scores.

min_n

Minimum contributing units per reference.

density_var

Column containing density objects.

normalize

Normalize each source map to unit sum, or retain its values.

transform

Optional log transformation after density-space aggregation. Log-space aggregation already returns log scores and requires "none".

Value

An eyesim_references object with keys, counts, source values, grouped sums and a specification. Use reference_map() to inspect one map, or sample_density() to score a table of locations carrying subject/item keys.

Details

self_item uses the target map; self_other_items averages that subject's other maps; others_item averages other subjects' maps of that item. others_other_items averages other items within each other subject, then averages those subject means equally, including in incomplete designs. min_n counts maps for self references and subjects for other references. Insufficient references retain their keys but return missing scores. Normalization precedes log transformation, which precedes aggregation.
